column2: Therefore by the gift of food all other gifts are given in full. Whatever gifts there are in the three worlds — enjoyments, women and vehicles,
food, drink and whatever lordship there is, Yudhishthira — all that is remembered as the fruit of giving food, here and hereafter,
since one whose limbs are nourished by food accumulates dharma. Food is pure, nectar, divine, clean, goodness itself, an elixir.
Food, drink, horse, cow with calf, bed, umbrella and sandals — these eight gifts are commended for the world of the dead, Yudhishthira.
By such special gifts men go at ease to the city of Dharmaraja; therefore one should practise dharma.
One should carefully give food, great king, and abundant water to the ancestors, and at the holy place of Amareshvara.
The holy places and sacred fields that have been declared grant desires and liberation here and accomplish every success;
of all of them the mother is declared to be the Narmada, best of rivers, auspicious, flowing through seven kalpas.
At other holy places austerity, sacrifices and gifts have a number; on the Narmada they have no number — so said Shankara.
As Shiva is, so the Reva is to be worshipped with effort. But those among these of evil deeds, sinful and without giving,
go by the dreadful southern path to Yama's abode. For eighty-six thousand yojanas all around
the city is to be known as most fierce, occupied by many forms; it seems near to men of cruel deeds.
Though far off, sinners go to it by a fierce path, set with sharp thorns and strewn with gravel,
made of sharp stones covered with razor edges; some by a great path with deadly splinters of wood,
here and there beset with fierce iron needles, uneven with trailing creepers, with mountains crowded with trees,
with blazing embers — they go along the road in misery. In places with uneven pits, hot clods and bricks,
with scorching sand and sharp stakes, covered here and there with many broken branches,
some go to Yama's abode through painful darkness, seized by hot embers on the road and by forest fires,
in places by heated rocks and mud up to the waist, in places full of foul water, in places with a fire of filthy dung,
in places with vultures, herons, tigers and most dreadful wicked insects, in places with great crabs and the like, in places again with pythons,
with fierce flies, in places with serpents of virulent poison, with herds of rutting elephants trampling all around,
with mighty sharp-horned beasts tearing up the path, with lions, horned buffaloes and fierce maddened beasts of prey,
with fierce dakinis and dreadful rakshasas, with most terrible diseases and unapproachable fires,
by a great fierce wind mixed with great flame, by a great rain of rocks, they are torn, without refuge;
in places scorched by burning heat they go on, torn on all sides by a great rain of arrows,
by falling masses of thunderbolts and dreadful meteors, struck by a rain of blazing embers they go on,
terrified again and again by most dreadful roars, filled all over by a rain of sharp weapons,
sprinkled again and again with streams of great salt water, by fierce great cold and by razor edges and the like,
and by others of many forms, in hundreds and thousands. Thus by a burning, fierce and uneven path,
great and without rest, O Bharata, painful and the abode of all sorrow,
all embodied beings, deluded and devoted to sin, are led by force by Yama's most dreadful messengers, who carry out Yama's command,
alone, dependent on others, without friends or kin, grieving over their own deeds and burning again and again,
mixed with ghosts and spirits, with throats, lips and palates dry, emaciated, terrified, burned by a blazing fire.
Some sinners, bound with chains and sinking deeply, are dragged burning by Yama's mighty messengers;
likewise, in misery, face down upon their chests, sinners are dragged bound by their hair;
in places embodied beings are pierced in the forehead with arrows and dragged; face up, by their sinful deeds, they are led along the evil road;
bound by the sides and arms, crushed in the belly, dragged by a noose around the neck, some go in great misery;
with a spike driven into the tongue and the nape drawn together, they are seized with a crescent-headed arrow and flung here and there;
others are bound with rope by the penis and testicles; with hands and feet cut off, with ears, lips and noses cut off,
with penis and testicles cut off, their heads and limbs hacked, pierced by goads and eaten by reptiles,
they run here and there crying, without refuge, struck again and again with hammers and iron rods,
and all around with dreadful whips of many kinds; they are pierced with slings, vomiting blood again and again;
thrown into water, they beg for shade. Thus men without giving go; but those who have made expiation,
taking provisions for the journey, go at ease to Yama's abode. Thus by the low road men reach Yama's city,
and are brought before Yama by the messengers as ordered. There Yama recalls to mind those of good deeds,
with welcome, the gift of a seat, foot-water, arghya and kindness: "You are blessed, great souls who have done good to yourselves,
you who have done good deeds for the sake of divine happiness, resorting to the bank of the Narmada at the mountain Amarakantaka,
giving gifts, practising austerity, making offerings and sacrifices according to rule, at Varanasi, Kurukshetra, Prayaga and Pushkara,
at Gaya, the Naimisha forest, the meeting of the Ganga and the sea, at Kedara, Bhairava, and Prabhasa with the moon-crested one,
in the lovely forest of Mahakala, at Shrishaila near Tripurantaka, at Traiyambaka, Dhautapapa and Nilakantha,
at Gangadvara, Himadvara and the mountain Kalanjara — at these and other holy places and fields in order —
you have gained the fruit of your birth, no doubt. Mount this chariot adorned with divine women and enjoyments
and go to the auspicious heaven endowed with every desire; there, having enjoyed great endless pleasures according to the measure of your merit,
you will also experience whatever little evil there is." I have told this much of those who dwell on the bank of the Kalpaga:
they mount chariots and stand above all. At all other holy places there is a number, as Brahma and the others said long ago;
whatever gift is given there, one is honoured in heaven by it; whoever dies there by the vow of fasting
goes, mounted on a divine chariot, to Shiva's abode. This I have told you, O king, the excellent merit of the Kalpaga.
Those of meritorious deeds see Yama as their own friend; but those of cruel deeds see him as terrifying,
his face dreadful with fangs, his eyes crooked with frowning brows, his hair standing up, with a great beard, his upper and lower lips quivering,
eighteen-armed, cruel, like a mass of dark collyrium, his hands raised with every weapon, roaring, staff in hand,
mounted on a great buffalo, his eyes like blazing fire, wearing red garlands and garments, risen up like the great Meru,
roaring like the clouds of dissolution, as if drinking the oceans, as if swallowing the three worlds and spewing out fire.
Death stands near him, radiant as the fire of time; Kala like collyrium, and the terrifying Kritanta;
sharp diseases of many kinds, of various terrifying forms, bearing spears, tridents and goads, with nooses, discuses and swords in their hands;
Yama's messengers, killers, fierce and cruel, like collyrium, with thunderbolt fangs, their hands raised with every weapon.
Such a Yama the evildoers see there; Yama goes quite fearlessly to the evildoer.
And the blessed Chitragupta, instructing them in dharma: "Ho, you of evil deeds, stealers of others' wealth,
proud of your looks and strength, violators of others' wives — whatever deed one does, one experiences it again.
Why then did you do evil to your own ruin? Why do you lament, tormented by your own deeds?
One's own deeds are experienced; no one else is at fault here. And these rulers of the earth have come, lord of the earth,
by their own dreadful deeds, proud in the strength of their evil wisdom. Ho, kings of wicked conduct, destroyers of your subjects,
why did you do that evil for a kingdom of brief duration? Whatever you seized through greed for kingship, delusion and unjust conduct,
enjoy its fruit as it truly is. Where is the kingdom or the wife for whose sake you did evil?
Leaving all that, you are now alone; your kinsmen, for whom you destroyed your subjects, do not see you.
Now, being cast down by Yama's messengers, how will it be?" With such words of many kinds they are received by Yama,
and they grieve over their own deeds, falling silent, O king. Having thus addressed those kings with words, the king of dharma then,
for the purification of their sin, said to his messengers: "Ho, Chanda, Mahachanda, seize these kings
and purify them of their sins in order with the fire of hell." Then quickly Yama's servants, seizing the kings by the feet,
whirled them round with speed and flung them down with great force on the scorching ground,
and dashed them against a great tree of iron; then they were all quickly battered by the blows,
and lay senseless and motionless, Yudhishthira; then, touched by the wind, they slowly revived again.
Bringing them for purification, they cast them into the ocean of hell. There are twenty-eight chief fierce crores of hells,
situated at the end of the seventh level in dreadful darkness: Atighora, Raudra, likewise Ghoratama,
the fifth, Atyantaduhkhajanani, of dreadful form; the sixth called Taranatara, the seventh Bhayanaka,
the eighth Kalaratri, the ninth Ghatotkata, the tenth Chanda, and below that Mahachanda,
Chandakolahala, Prachanda, Paragnika, Jaghanya, Avara, Loma, Bhishani, Nayika,
Karala, Vikarala, resting on twenty thunderbolts, Asta, Panchakona, Sudirgha, Parivartula,
Saptabhauma, Ashtabhauma, and another here, Dirghamaya — thus by name are declared the dreadful crores of hells.
These twenty-eight are remembered according to the measure of beings; of them in order five leaders each are to be known,
for each of all the crores, by name, lord of the people. Raurava is the first of them, where embodied beings weep;
with the torments of Maharaurava even the great weep; Tamas, Shita and Ushna — these five are remembered as leaders.
Aghora first, Tikshna, Padma, Sanjivana, Shatha, Mahamaya, Viloma, Kantaka and Kataka are remembered;
Tivra, Vama, Karala, Kinkarala, Prakampana, Mahachakra, Supadma, Kalasutra, Pragarjana,
Suchimukha, Sunemi, Khadaka, Suprapidita, Kumbhipaka, Supaka and the most dreadful Krakacha,
Angararatri, Pachana, Asrikpuyabhava, Sutikshna, Shandashakuni, Mahasamvartaka, Kratu,
Taptajantu, Pankalesha, Putiman, Hradastrapu, Uchchhvasa, Niruchchhvasa, Sudirgha, Krurashalmali,
Ushtrita, Mahanada, Pravaha, Supravahana, Vrishashraya, Vrishashva, and those with the faces of lions, tigers and elephants,
with the faces of dogs, boars, goats, buffaloes, rams, mice and donkeys, with the mouths of sharks, crocodiles and alligators, most dreadful and terrifying,
Sarvabhaksha, Svabhaksha, Sarvakarma, Ashvavayasa, Gridhroluka, Uluka, Shardula, Kapi, Kachchhura,
Gandaka, Putivaktra, Raktasya, Putimutrika, Kanadhumra, Tusharagni, Krimiman and Niraya,
Atodya, Pratodya, Rudhirodya, Bhojana, Kalatmaga, Anubhaksha and the most dreadful Sarvabhaksha,
Karkata, Vishala, Vikata, Katapūtana, Ambarisha, Kataha and the painful river Vaitarani,
Sutapta, Lohashanku, Ekapada, Ashrupurana, the dreadful Asipatravana and the established Asthilinga,
the presses for sesame, linseed and sugarcane, Kutapapapramardana, Mahachulli, Vichulli and the stone of heated iron,
the mountain called Kshuradhara, Maya, Yamalaparvata, Suchi, Vishtha, Andhakupa, Patana and Patana,
Mushali, Vrishali, Ashiva and Sankatala, Talapatrasigahana and Mahamohaka,
Sammohana, Asthibhanga, Taptachalamaya, Aguna, Bahuduhkha, Mahaduhkha, Kashmala and Yamala,
Halahala, Virupa, Shvarupa, Chyutamanasa, Ekapada, Tripada, Tivra and then Vidita.
These twenty-eight are remembered in order as the groups of five.
They brood on their own deeds and stand silent and motionless; then in order, with fire-coloured iron rods set with thorns,
they are struck hard on the head by Yama's messengers; then in a well full of excrement, the home of worms,
the sinners are cooked all around by dreadful servants; then with salt water and in fire especially,
they are cooked like aubergines in a heated iron cauldron; thrown into a well of filth crowded with water creatures,
and then cast into a pool full of fat, blood and pus, they are eaten by sharp worms and iron-beaked crows;
they are cooked like meat on heaps of blazing embers; men full of sin are impaled on sharp stakes;
those sinners are cooked in many ways by Yama's messengers, then again in cauldrons full of scorching oil.
The tongues of those who speak untruth and unkindness are torn out, pressed hard on the chest with a very firm, heated foot;
and likewise of the brahmin who applies false scripture — his wide belly, filled with the wealth of sacrifice, is pierced with sharp spears.
The mouths of those fools who revile mother and father are filled again and again with sand and sprinkled,
then again and again with blazing lye water, and their mouths are quickly filled to the brim with hot oil.
With excrement full of worms, trampled by soldiers' feet like dogs, crushed with a horn, they enter the iron shalmali tree;
they are struck again on the back by fearsome, mighty ones; with a very blunt, strong, toothed saw
they are split from the head down, by the dreadful deeds born of themselves; they are made to eat their own flesh and drink their own blood.
The fools who did not give food and drink, nor even approved of it, are crushed like sugarcane, battered with hammers;
in the dreadful forest of sword-palms they are cut to pieces; their whole bodies pierced with needles, they are then impaled on stakes,
and dragged about writhing, yet they do not die; their flesh is torn from their bodies and their bones with hammers,
and they are dragged about swiftly many times by Yama's mighty messengers. Without breath they remain long in hell without breathing,
and breathing always, their mouths filled with sand; in the Rauravas they are tormented in the teeth by many kinds of agents;
with the torments of Maharaurava even the great weep. On the private parts, anus, side, feet, chest and head
they are struck by soldiers with sharp, heated iron hammers. Women who revile others' wives by their looks and laugh at them,
who embrace other husbands and do not care for their own: "Why do you run so fast? You did not remember what is eternal;
you deceived your husband, blind with sin, at your pleasure" — they are thrown into an iron pot and slowly heaped up,
cooked in a fierce fire and pushed into rocks, flung into blind wells and bitten hard by pythons.
Those who revile the great-souled teacher who shows dharma, the devotee of Shiva, the brahmin and the eternal dharma of Shiva —
they are pinned by Yama's servants with spikes on the chest and throat, on the tongue, at the joints of the body and through the lips.
Such and other most dreadful torments of sinners are to be known in each single hell by the hundreds and thousands.
The torments of all sinners are deep, O king; thus the torments in all the hells are endless.
What man could tell them even in a hundred years? Thus, cast down by their own many dreadful deeds,
they are cooked in order in all the hells, no doubt; and the great sinners in all the hells
are tormented by many agents as long as the moon and stars endure; and likewise all sinners always in these hells
are cooked in the four directions in the hells, no doubt; men guilty of lesser sins go to half of that.
Death is not known, dear one, when it will come to whom; when death comes suddenly, what man gets another year?
Since, leaving everything, you will surely go alone, therefore be devoted to truth and dharma with every effort.
I have told you all this, the characteristics of the hells.
The excellent story of the Narmada was told by the Sun, out of my father's compassion for the gods and ancestors;
a lakh and a quarter and more were told to Ravi by Brahma; there I heard all of it, and Brahma heard it from Shiva;
it was told long ago by Shiva to Parvati and Shanmukha. Whoever, having reached Jambudvipa and taken a human birth,
does not resort to the goddess Narmada who flows through seven kalpas — by bathing, immersing, drinking, and the acts of giving and the like,
what other in this world gives a goal to those whose minds are struck by sin? Those who meditate on the great goddess Narmada, remover of sin —
their sins perish as darkness at sunrise. Whoever remembers the Narmada or praises her with the voice,
on reaching the other world is not harassed by Yama's messengers. Whoever praises the Narmada, even a sinful, vile man,
never passes into the hells appointed by rule. The Ganga and other rivers and crores of holy places there, in many ways,
are at once purified by the radiance and power of the Reva. Whoever in hell remembers the Mekala, Hara or Hari
is at once released by Yama's messengers, no doubt. If on the Vaidurya mountain at Amarakantaka
stands Omkara, the supreme Lord who gives the fruit of enjoyment and liberation, why do those whose minds are struck by sin grieve here?
Siddheshvara, the Siddhalinga that bestows grace on the worlds, Yajneshvara in the middle, and the moon-crested one right there,
and on the southern side of the Narmada the linga Maheshvara, and the fourth, Kapilesha — the wise know this as Shiva's field.
Those who always worship with devotion, with flowers, incense, lights and libations, go to Shiva's world, not to the hells, no doubt.
I have told you all this as you asked, sinless one; he told of the most sinful men who do not abide in dharma, O Bharata.
The gift of a cow, the gift of gold, the gift of sesame likewise, the gift of food, the gift of milk and all household goods,
and the gift of temples and gardens — the best of men who make these do not go to Yama's world or to the dreadful hell;
they are freed from all sins, as is Shiva's word. Honour is seized by dishonour, the meeting with the beloved by separation,
youth by old age, happiness by hardship; the body is battered by wrinkles and grey hairs —
what can a wise man do when battered by old age? The youth and beauty of woman and man, which please each other,
when seized by old age please neither. Seeing himself as never before, full of slackness,
whoever does not become dispassionate — who is more senseless than he? A man overcome by old age, by his wife, sons and other kin,
and by wicked servants, is despised because of his weakness. One afflicted by old age is not able to accomplish dharma, wealth, desire or liberation;
therefore one should practise dharma beforehand. The imbalance of wind, bile, phlegm and the rest, Yudhishthira,
and the aggregate of wind and the rest, is declared to be born of the body; therefore this body of one's own is to be known as given over to disease.
Afflicted by an excess of wind and by fever, by diseases arising from many causes, one has many kinds of great sorrow;
these are known to oneself — what else shall I tell? A hundred and one deaths are established in this body;
one of them is in the form of time, the rest are remembered as accidental; those called accidental here are quelled by medicines,
and by japa, fire offering and gifts; but death by time is not quelled. Untimely death for everyone arises from poison and the like;
and no great man fears untimely death because of it. Various painful diseases, creatures with their physicians,
poisons and hostile magic are the doors of death for embodied beings. Even Dhanvantari himself, though one is afflicted by diseases, snakes and the like,
cannot make well an embodied being whose time has come. Neither medicine, austerity, gifts, friends nor kin
are able to save one oppressed by time. There is no sorrow equal to death, no enemy equal to death,
no time equal to death for all embodied beings. A good wife, sons, friends, kingdom, lordship and pleasures —
death cuts them all off, of whatever kind, O Bharata. This I have told you, O king, the kin and the worldly existence hard to cross.
Knowing the outcome, that all is the food of time, therefore the Kalpaga of seven kalpas is to be served with every effort,
ever removing all sorrow and destroying all grief; whatever desires one desires, the goddess grants them.
This is knowledge, this is meditation, learning and knowing the Veda — the Kalpaga of seven kalpas, the dwelling of all beings, is to be served.
Sacrifice, giving, austerity, truth, Vedic study and libations to the ancestors — he who resorts to the water of the Reva obtains their fruit.
Thousands of brahmakurchas and ten thousand drinkings of Soma are not equal to a sixteenth part of drinking the water of the Narmada.
Even one bound by great sins committed in many births is freed at once by reciting at the dreadful southern side of Omkara.
No gift is renowned in the three worlds as higher than the gift of a cow; whoever, having bathed in the water of the Narmada, gives a cow to a brahmin —
even the gods cannot properly reckon its measure.
a load of gold, adorned with ornaments and all jewels. The brahmin sage named Mudgala, established himself in Brahman,
and all the brahmins of Mudgala's line, devoted to truth and dharma, a hundred and eight and more brahmins who expound Brahman —
to them Harishchandra gave at the conjunction of Rahu and the sun, having duly honoured the brahmins, filled with supreme faith,
and having worshipped Maheshana, the place of supreme success, and Chakrapani Hrishikesha, filled with supreme joy,
at the Sarasvati, best of kings, with sesame and darbha; by the power of this gift all the worlds were won by him.
A city in the atmosphere, charming to all worlds, was obtained, renowned as Harishchandrapuri in this world of moving and unmoving.
Adorned with truth, giving, renunciation of all and the like, a king equal to Harishchandra has not been nor will be —
thus a verse was sung long ago by Shakra and the best of gods. Shashanka too did all this, resorting to the bank of the Narmada —
gifts, sacrifice, austerity and truth at the mountain Amarakantaka; and he gave a cow in the act of calving to a great-souled brahmin.
By the power of this gift he surpassed Harishchandra, burning up the sin of many births as fire burns a heap of cotton.
As long as the calf's two feet and mouth are seen at the womb, so long the cow is to be known as the earth with its mountains, forests and woods.
With golden horns, silver hooves, with its calf and a bronze milking pail, joined with a bath in the Narmada, with kusha and sesame —
between Omkara and Amara, at Kotitirtha, the lord of men gave a thousand of these to the brahmins.
Meanwhile the drums of the gods sounded in the sky; at that moment, mounted on a vehicle blazing as with masses of gems,
praised by countless beings in chariots nearby, with a golden umbrella held over him and fanned with chowries —
Harishchandra stood a thousand yojanas below. Seeing such a deed of Shashanka, lord of the people,
he reproached Kurukshetra, his mind filled with wonder: "The gift given by Shashanka on the great river at the conjunction of Rahu and Soma
must not be ordinary" — in brief. His face downcast, Harishchandra, best of kings,
went quickly to Brahma's world, where the lord of the worlds dwells, and having duly saluted him, asked the Grandsire:
The gods have been surpassed in giving by the great-souled Shashanka. What merit is this, O Brahma, that surpasses Kurukshetra?
The holy place named Amareshvara, arising from the Reva — nothing has equalled it; it shines ever higher.
Hearing the words of the wise Harishchandra, Brahma spoke to Harishchandra, best of kings:

Give up despondency, king of kings; the course of karma is deep. A king like Shashanka I have neither seen nor heard of.

skandapuran:55:30	according to rule at the mountain Amarakantaka; at the conjunction of Rahu and the sun, lakhs of holy places, O Bharata —
skandapuran:55:31	the Sarasvati, Kurukshetra, Pushkara, Naimisha and these other holy places — came to bathe
skandapuran:55:32	in the Mekala at Kotitirtha, Harishchandra, lord of men. Give up thinking any holy place equal to the Mekala, king of kings.
skandapuran:55:33	I weighed Kurukshetra against Varanasi long ago; holy places do not equal the power of this holy place.
skandapuran:55:34	Kurukshetra is merely famous, keeping the world's pilgrimages going. Those who have not heard the Purana, full of false knowledge —
skandapuran:55:35	let them serve the goddess Kalpaga, if they desire the supreme state. Having bowed to the Creator, the lord of Ayodhya then,
filled with supreme joy, went to Amareshvara. All this has been told to you as it is, man of good vows;
the man who hears it, O king, gains the fruit of a thousand cows.
He held in his heart day and night this six-syllabled mantra, "Om namah Shivaya," the very best of all mantras.
Knowing his supreme devotion, the god of gods, husband of Uma, the blessed trident-bearer, came in visible form.
The god spoke to Matanga, O Bharata: "Choose a boon — blessings on you — for this meditation, man of good vows."
Matanga said: "If you are pleased, lord of gods, and wish to give a boon here, let this holy place be renowned by the name Matanga.
Chandalas, dog-eaters, and those in sinful births, even without japa and the like, let them be freed here from sin.
The linga named Matanga rests on the bank of the Narmada; whoever bathes here and worships it, let his bonds be released.
This I regard as the boon by your grace, Maheshvara." Hearing his words, the husband of Shiva's consort replied:
Let all this be so by my grace, no doubt. Having said this, the god went to Kailasa, best of mountains.
Having received the boon, Matanga, mounted on a vehicle that went at will, adorned with every ornament, to the city of Uma and Maheshvara
went quickly to enjoy pleasures for long by the power of the bath. On the new moon of Chaitra, and on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight,
whatever is offered and given there obtains endless fruit; by giving sesame water, even those in sinful births —
whoever gladdens the ancestors with a pinda rich in barley meal and jaggery, his ancestors are satisfied for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Whoever worships the linga with sesame and rice mixed is honoured in Shiva's world for thousands of years.
The holy place Matanga is called the Ashoka grove; it has been told you, on the northern bank of the Reva, O Bharata.
Now I shall tell of another situated on the southern side, the holy place named Mrigavana, destroyer of all sins.
Bathing there, one should worship Vishnu bearing conch, discus and mace; on the eleventh day, great king, one should pass the night fasting,
and worship Hari there at Mrigavana with fragrance and flowers; when one brahmin is fed there, let a lakh be fed.
By giving sesame water the ancestors reach Vishnu's state. Situated right there is the excellent holy place Varaha,
where the earth was raised up in the form of the Boar, and another, Vishvarupa, by Hari of boundless radiance.
A chaste wife and a woman who fasts for a month, bathing there according to rule, attain Vishnu's world.
And by him the forest filled with deer and tigers was burned; all of it became ashes and entirely dust.
When the rains had come, in the auspicious stream of the Narmada, when the sun was in Virgo, on the twelfth under Shravana,
through contact with the water of the Narmada the serpents became yakshas; at once they had divine bodies and mounted Vishnu's vehicle.
That hunter became a king by the power of this holy place and enjoyed charming pleasures for ten thousand years.
The deer that were burned there also attained the state of gandharvas and reached Vishnu's state by Vishnu's vehicle.
Whoever gives up his life there, helplessly or willingly, rejoices in Vishnu's world for a thousand divine years.
By giving sesame water the ancestors reach the supreme goal. Another holy place named Manoratha gives supreme success,
renowned in the three worlds, arising on the bank of the Reva; whatever desire a man prays for, having merely bathed,
he obtains it all by the power of this holy place. The meeting of the Angaravarta gives the fruit of a thousand cows;
the god Angareshvara stands at that confluence; a man who merely bathes there attains the leadership of ganas.
When Mars falls on the fourth day, O Bharata, one should make a golden man and wrap it in red cloth,
with a copper vessel filled with ghee and with jaggery; all that one should give according to rule, especially to a learned brahmin.
By the power of the gift and the holy place one shares half of Shakra's throne. Since sins bring sorrows, fierce and many,
therefore sin should not be committed, for it causes one's own torment. At whatever time and place and at whatever age
good or evil karma is done, so is it experienced by that person. Therefore one should always give without interruption to the needy;
otherwise enjoyments are cut off like small streams in summer. As the auspicious goddess who flows through seven kalpas is served,
for the cutting off of worldly existence I tell you the yoga of knowledge: knowledge that reveals Shiva, and yoga reflected on there.
Yoga, whose course is hard to know, is in the presence of the Narmada and Shiva; Shiva's command operates there, as does the rule of bathing and worship.
Without conflict with its doctrine, one should not contradict it with books; a man obtains dharma and knowledge together for the sake of liberation.
With earlier and later in conflict, where would the intended meaning be? Having seen reasoning from its root, one should reject what conflicts with Shruti.
Therefore the wise should always examine the meaning of the self with the help of the Agama, and not by inference alone.
The fruit of the low, the high and the rest is remembered as manifold and one's own; therefore one should examine merit, the good and the greatly fruitful.
The wise man should avoid from afar heretics, those of wrong conduct, hypocrites who keep the cat's vow, deceivers, sophists and revilers of holy places,
the naked ascetics, the white-robed and other disputers by reasoning; with them there should be no conversation nor any contact.
In the Kali age dharma is reversed; the naked, shaven ones eat filth; therefore, leaving that, one should practise the dharma of the Treta.
In all dharmas the authority is what Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva have declared; whoever does otherwise surely falls into hell.
This is the conclusion of all the shastras: the goddess Kalpaga is to be served always by those devoted to Shiva's worship.
One should offer libations to the ancestors and give alms to the mendicant; compassion to all beings and reflection on the story of the Narmada —
this is the whole of knowledge, purifying all actions. The lord without beginning, middle or end, pure by nature,
all-knowing and perfect, is to be known as Shiva in Shiva's Agama; the knowledge that accomplishes all aims is taught by him, without doubt.
Shiva, who is all-knowing, perfect, pure by nature and free of all faults — how could he speak otherwise?
Without Shiva's command how could there be the creation of the world? Because primal matter is insentient and the Purusha ignorant,
primal matter, atoms and whatever is insentient cannot of themselves be agent or seer without an intelligent instrument;
just as a lump of clay does not of itself become a pot, so nature would not stand of itself without command and intelligence.
Instruction in dharma and adharma and the weighing of dharma and adharma are never established in the first creation without the all-knowing one.
As this dreadful ocean of worldly existence has flowed from beginningless time, so Shiva too is beginningless and remembered as the releaser from worldly existence.
As medicine is by nature the opponent of diseases, so Shiva is remembered as the opponent of the dread of worldly existence.
As the sick suffer helplessly without a physician, so without Shiva the whole world is helpless.
Therefore the beginningless, all-knowing, perfect supreme Shiva exists; there is no other deliverer of man in the ocean of worldly existence.
Those devoted to Shiva who practise the knowledge of Shiva in their hearts — if the Vedas are authoritative, knowledge arises in them.
And this Narmada is the refuge of all beings on earth, the goddess who in the form of water bestows grace on the worlds.
The moving and unmoving, the fourfold host of beings — the blessed one surely lifts them up when they are falling into hell.
Knowing this, best of men, and looking to Shiva and the Kalpaga, one should give to brahmins tall divine houses furnished with wealth and grain,
divine with all furnishings. To a helpless, very old or infirm man with a family,
whoever gives a brahmin a house of wood and clay — and whoever has such lovely houses built all around Amarakantaka,
divine ones — hear the fruit of his merit: what need has he of many gifts given, O Bharata?
This alone is the supreme gift, accomplishing every desire and aim; the man who hears it with devotion is freed from all sins.
Markandeya said: Listen; having bowed to Maheshvara, I shall tell of the supreme world of the cow-mothers, endowed with every desire,
situated as it is above all the worlds. Then the seven netherworlds, and the netherworld likewise;
as great as the extent of the earth's surface all around, so great is its extent, and the oceans too;
the height of each of them is declared: five thousand yojanas, successively;
its inner height is a thousand yojanas; the openings of all of them are remembered as nine thousand.
Their lovely greatness by name on earth: endowed with the most divine things, with the radiance of glorious gold,
the king of serpents always dwells there, having made his home in it — Ananta, of endless abode, Mukunda, Nripashaivala.
Then there is the one named Rasatala, a ground that delights Shiva; there is the lovely great city of Vasuki, king of the serpents,
and the great city of Suraloman, lord of the danavas, and of Suparna and of all the great-souled daityas.
Then there is the one named Sutala, its ground set with gravel; there always dwell the nagas and the Svastikas,
and there too is the supreme abode of the lords of the danavas, the great-souled Vairochana, Hiranya and others.
Then it is called Atala, of those netherworlds; above all of them the surface of the earth is of clay.
There is the great city of Kalanemi, lord of the asuras, shining with lovely gold, and another of Vainateya.
Then there is the netherworld named Vitala, with red ground; in it is the abode made by the lord of the danavas named Mahantaka.
